title: Broth Lab
description: The base that decides almost everything else about a bowl -- clear or cloudy, light or rich. Explore the styles, then see how boil method, bones, time, and fat each push a broth in a different direction.

concepts.definition: A clear broth style, simmered gently so it stays transparent rather than emulsifying.
A cloudy, emulsified broth style, boiled hard enough for fat and collagen to blend into the liquid itself.
A paitan-style broth made specifically from pork bones -- the most internationally recognized version of the technique.
A lighter-aroma alternative to pork, usable as either a clear chintan or, boiled hard, its own paitan (tori paitan).
Ramen's most common animal base -- can be kept clear and light or boiled into a rich, cloudy tonkotsu.
Usually niboshi (dried sardines) simmered alongside or instead of an animal bone base, for a briny depth.
An animal-free base, less common in traditional ramen but increasingly seen in modern shops. Not yet represented by a canonical style in this Encyclopedia.
A kelp-based umami stock, often layered underneath a lighter shoyu or shio broth rather than used alone.

options.label: Gentle Simmer
options.effect: Keeps the broth clear and light -- the chintan approach behind shoyu and shio styles.

options.label: Hard Rolling Boil
options.effect: Emulsifies fat and collagen into a cloudy, rich broth -- the paitan/tonkotsu approach.

options.label: Chicken
options.effect: A lighter, rounder aroma than pork -- can go clear or, boiled hard, its own creamy tori paitan.

options.label: Pork
options.effect: The most common ramen base -- sharp and porky when boiled hard, mild when simmered gently.

options.label: Seafood (Niboshi)
options.effect: Adds a briny, savory depth without much body of its own -- usually paired with a lighter animal base.

options.label: Kombu / Dashi Only
options.effect: The lightest option -- pure umami with almost no body, usually a supporting layer rather than the whole broth.

options.label: Short (1-3 hrs)
options.effect: Enough for a light, clean stock -- not enough time to build real body.

options.label: Medium (4-6 hrs)
options.effect: A fuller-bodied broth, common for standard shoyu and shio styles.

options.label: Long (8-12+ hrs)
options.effect: Long enough to fully emulsify a hard-boiled pork base into a dense, rich tonkotsu.

options.label: Lean
options.effect: A thin, brothy mouthfeel that lets the tare and dashi lead.

options.label: Moderate
options.effect: A balanced body -- enough fat to coat the noodle without feeling heavy.

options.label: Rich
options.effect: A thick, coating mouthfeel -- the fat itself becomes part of the broth's identity.

title: Noodle Lab
description: What actually makes a ramen noodle a ramen noodle -- not pasta, not udon. See how kansui, hydration, thickness, and shape change the noodle rather than crunching a recipe.

concepts.definition: Higher-protein wheat flour builds more gluten, which is what gives ramen noodles their structure and chew.
The ratio of water to flour in the dough -- lower hydration makes a firmer, chewier noodle; higher hydration makes a softer, more tender one.
Alkaline mineral water added to the dough -- the single ingredient that separates a ramen noodle from a plain wheat noodle or pasta.
The pH effect kansui has on the dough -- it firms the gluten structure and gives the noodle its pale yellow tint and springy bite.
How thick or wide a noodle is cut, chosen to match the broth it's meant to carry.
Whether a noodle is cut straight or curly -- curly noodles hold more broth in each bite; straight noodles cook more evenly.

options.label: None
options.effect: Without kansui, the noodle is closer to plain wheat pasta than true ramen -- soft, with none of the characteristic springiness.

options.label: Standard
options.effect: The typical amount used across most regional styles -- a clear, springy bite and pale yellow color.

options.label: High-Alkaline
options.effect: A firmer, more assertive bite and a more pronounced mineral aroma -- common in noodles built to stand up to very rich broths.

options.label: Low (~30%)
options.effect: A firm, dense, chewy noodle -- common in thin styles meant to be eaten quickly, like Hakata's.

options.label: Medium (~35%)
options.effect: A balanced texture -- neither especially firm nor especially soft.

options.label: High (~40%+)
options.effect: A softer, more tender noodle with a looser structure -- typical of thick, high-hydration styles like Kitakata's.

options.label: Thin
options.effect: Cooks fast and stays light -- suited to delicate broths and kaedama-style refills.

options.label: Medium
options.effect: The most broadly compatible width -- works with most broth styles without disappearing or overwhelming.

options.label: Thick
options.effect: Substantial enough to stand up to a heavy, rich broth without going limp.

options.label: Straight
options.effect: Cooks evenly and reads cleanly against a clear broth.

options.label: Curly
options.effect: Traps more broth in each curl -- a noticeably different eating experience bite to bite.

title: Tare Lab
description: The seasoning base that actually defines a bowl's identity -- added to the bottom of the bowl before broth, not simmered into the stockpot. See how tare and broth are meant to work together.

concepts.definition: A soy-sauce-based tare, ramen's most common seasoning base -- usually blended with mirin, sake, or a touch of sugar.
A salt-based tare, kept simple so a broth's own clarity and delicacy stay the focus.
A fermented-soybean-paste tare -- the boldest, most assertive of the three major tare families.
How much salt a tare contributes overall -- the primary lever for how bold or restrained a finished bowl tastes.
The savory depth a tare adds on top of its base saltiness, often from fermentation or added dashi components.
Both shoyu and miso are fermented products -- the fermentation itself is what gives them complexity beyond simple saltiness.
Garlic, ginger, and other aromatics sometimes stirred into tare directly, layering a second flavor dimension under the broth.

options.label: Shoyu
options.effect: Balanced, savory, and the most broadly compatible with different broth styles.

options.label: Shio
options.effect: The most restrained option -- lets a delicate, clear broth carry the bowl.

options.label: Miso
options.effect: The boldest, most fermented-forward option -- built to stand up to rich, heavy broths.

options.label: Light
options.effect: A gentle seasoning that keeps the broth itself in the spotlight.

options.label: Medium
options.effect: A standard, well-balanced seasoning level.

options.label: Bold
options.effect: An assertive, forward seasoning -- risks overwhelming a delicate broth if not matched carefully.

options.label: None
options.effect: A clean, unadorned tare flavor.

options.label: Garlic-Ginger
options.effect: Adds a warm, savory aromatic layer, common in miso-style tare.

options.label: Citrus
options.effect: A bright, sharp lift -- less traditional, more often seen in modern shops.

title: Aroma Oil Lab
description: A small amount of floated fat that changes a bowl's first impression more than almost anything else. See how the choice of oil shifts a bowl's whole character.

concepts.definition: A light, rounded fat, often used to add richness without a strong pork character.
A rich, savory rendered fat, one of the most common ramen aroma oils.
Oil infused with scallion, adding a sharp, fresh aromatic note without much richness.
Garlic (and often ginger) stir-fried into fat -- Sapporo miso's signature aroma oil.
A spicy, toasted chili-infused oil, adding both heat and aroma.
Toasted or lightly burnt black garlic oil -- Kumamoto ramen's defining, most intense aroma oil.

options.label: Chicken Fat
options.effect: Rounds out a broth without adding a strong pork note -- a common finish for lighter or chicken-based bowls.

options.label: Pork Fat
options.effect: A savory, classic richness -- the default aroma oil for most tonkotsu-adjacent bowls.

options.label: Scallion Oil
options.effect: A sharp, fresh lift with very little added richness -- good for keeping a bowl feeling light.

options.label: Garlic Oil
options.effect: A warm, savory aroma that becomes part of a bowl's core identity rather than a background note.

options.label: Chili Oil (Rayu)
options.effect: Adds real heat alongside a toasted aroma -- changes a bowl's character more than almost any other single addition.

options.label: Mayu (Black Garlic Oil)
options.effect: The most intense, assertive option -- built to be noticed, and easy to let dominate a delicate broth if overused.

options.label: Light Drizzle
options.effect: A subtle background note -- the broth itself still leads.

options.label: Standard
options.effect: A noticeable but balanced presence -- the typical amount used across most shops.

options.label: Heavy
options.effect: The oil becomes the first thing you notice -- appropriate for bold styles, risky on delicate ones.

title: Ajitama Lab
description: The marinated soft-boiled egg that shows up on nearly every shoyu bowl -- a small technique with very little room for error. See how cooking time, cooling, and marinade each shape the result.

concepts.definition: How long the egg boils before cooling -- the single biggest lever over how set or runny the yolk ends up.
The spectrum from fully liquid to fully firm -- ajitama is usually aimed at a jammy, half-set middle ground.
An immediate ice bath stops the carryover cooking that would otherwise keep firming the yolk after the egg leaves the pot.
Fresher eggs are harder to peel cleanly than eggs a few days old, since the membrane bonds more tightly to a very fresh shell.
A soy-based liquid -- usually shoyu, mirin, and sake or dashi -- that the peeled egg sits in to take on color and flavor.
How concentrated the marinade is -- too strong and only the outer white turns salty and rubbery before the yolk takes on any flavor at all.
How long the peeled egg actually sits in the marinade -- flavor works inward slowly, so time and salinity are linked.
Ajitama keep marinating the whole time they sit in the liquid, so a batch left too long will eventually oversalt even at a mild concentration.

options.label: 6 Minutes
options.effect: A mostly liquid, deeply jammy yolk -- delicate to handle and easy to overcook by even 30 seconds.

options.label: 7 Minutes
options.effect: The classic ajitama target -- a soft, half-set yolk that holds together when sliced.

options.label: 9 Minutes
options.effect: A firmer, custard-like yolk -- more forgiving to handle, less of the classic jammy pull.

options.label: Immediate Ice Bath
options.effect: Stops cooking instantly -- the yolk stays exactly where the cooking time left it.

options.label: No Ice Bath
options.effect: Carryover heat keeps cooking the yolk for another minute or more -- a 7-minute egg can drift toward a 9-minute result.

options.label: Classic Shoyu-Mirin-Sake
options.effect: The standard, balanced ajitama flavor -- savory with a touch of sweetness.

options.label: Dashi-Diluted (Lighter)
options.effect: A gentler, more savory-forward marinade that colors the egg more slowly.

options.label: Chili-Infused
options.effect: A modern variation that adds real heat on top of the classic base -- not traditional, but increasingly common.

options.label: 2-4 Hours
options.effect: A light tint and mild flavor -- mostly on the surface, barely into the white.

options.label: Overnight
options.effect: The most common target -- flavor reaches through the white with the yolk still mild and jammy.

options.label: 2+ Days
options.effect: Deep color and flavor throughout, but risks an oversalted white and a firmer overall texture the longer it sits.

title: Chashu Lab
description: Ramen's signature pork topping, and one with real, legitimate regional variation -- there's no single correct method. See how cut, cooking method, and rolling each change the result.

concepts.definition: Pork belly and pork shoulder are the two most common cuts -- belly for fat and richness, shoulder for a leaner, chewier bite.
Rolling a slab of belly or shoulder and tying it before cooking produces even, round slices -- an optional step, not a requirement.
Slow-cooking the pork directly in a seasoned liquid (often shoyu, mirin, sake, and aromatics) until tender, soaking up flavor as it cooks.
Cooking the pork dry, often glazed, closer to Chinese char siu -- a firmer texture with browned, caramelized edges rather than a liquid-soaked one.
Most chashu takes its flavor from the braising liquid itself rather than a dry rub, though roasted versions may use both.
Ranges from soft and falling-apart tender (long, slow braise) to firmer and slightly chewy (shorter cook, leaner cut).
Chashu is sliced thin to be eaten in a bite or two, not served as a standalone cut of meat.
Usually served cold or room-temperature slices laid over hot noodles and broth, which warms them through at the table.

Belly vs. shoulder, braised vs. roasted, rolled vs. flat -- all are real, established approaches used across different shops and regions, not a single 'correct' method with everything else a shortcut.

options.label: Pork Belly
options.effect: Rich and fatty, with visible fat layers running through each slice -- the most common chashu cut.

options.label: Pork Shoulder
options.effect: Leaner and slightly firmer, with more distinct chew -- a common alternative where a lighter bowl calls for it.

options.label: Braised
options.effect: Long, slow cooking directly in seasoned liquid -- tender, soaked through with flavor, falls apart easily.

options.label: Roasted
options.effect: Dry-cooked and often glazed -- firmer texture, caramelized edges, closer to Chinese char siu.

options.label: Rolled & Tied
options.effect: Produces uniform, round slices with an even fat-to-meat ratio in every piece.

options.label: Flat (Untied)
options.effect: A more rustic result -- irregular slices, but simpler prep with one less step.

options.label: Thin
options.effect: Delicate slices that warm through quickly in the hot broth and disappear in a bite or two.

options.label: Thick
options.effect: A more substantial, chewier bite -- common at shops that treat chashu as a bigger part of the bowl.
